name: Scope
text: Adopt the dual-log system with a write-through checksum plus a background reconciliation worker now. Two fully independent logs run in parallel, each record carrying a checksum of its content and the last write’s logical clock. The reconciliation worker streams diffs in real time, blocking writes only when a proven mismatch is found—no central validator to fail, no silent corruption, and no blind spots. The trade-off is accepting a small latency hit on reconciled writes when splits occur.

name: Scriv
text: The write-through checksum plus background reconciliation still risks silent corruption if the reconciliation worker lags behind a fast split—user writes can race ahead before the diffs catch up. Instead, run two independent logs with a *write-through version vector* plus a *read-time conflict detector*: any read that hits a mismatch blocks until the logs reconcile, proving correctness before the user sees stale data. Settle it with a 24-hour load test injecting 10% write skew—if no corruption surfaces and p99 reads stay under 50ms, the version vector wins.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the dual-log system with a write-through checksum plus a background reconciliation worker now. Two fully independent logs run in parallel, each record carries a checksum of the write, and a background worker streams real-time diffs to surface splits instantly—no race can hide corruption because the checksum mismatch blocks reads until reconciled. The trade-off is accepting a small latency hit on writes while the worker catches up, but it guarantees no silent data loss and no central validator to fail.

name: Scriv
text: The write-through checksum plus background reconciliation still risks silent corruption if the reconciliation worker falls behind under load—user data can diverge for minutes before the diffs catch up. Instead, run two independent logs with a *write-through version vector* *and* a *read-time validator* that compares clocks on every read; if they mismatch, fail the read and log the event for immediate repair. Settle it with a 24-hour load test simulating worst-case skew—if the validator blocks no more than 0.1% of reads, adopt it.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the dual-log system with a write-through checksum plus a background reconciliation worker now. Two fully independent logs run in parallel, and every record carries a checksum—any mismatch surfaces instantly during reads or reconciliation, eliminating blind spots without a central validator. The trade-off is accepting a small performance hit from checksum computation and reconciliation latency, but it guarantees no silent corruption.

name: Sift
text: The write-through checksum plus background reconciliation still risks silent corruption if the checksum itself races ahead of the write—user data can diverge before the diff worker sees the split. Instead, enforce a *synchronous dual-write with a quorum lock*: both logs must acknowledge the write before the client proceeds, and the reconciliation worker only audits after. Settle it with a 24-hour chaos test injecting 100ms network splits between the two logs—if no corruption surfaces, the quorum lock holds.

name: Scriv
text: The write-through checksum plus background reconciliation still risks silent corruption if the checksum itself is wrong or the reconciliation worker misses a split—user data can diverge for hours before detection. Instead, run two independent logs with a *write-back version vector* and a *durable commit log*: each write carries the last write’s logical clock, and the commit log blocks until both logs acknowledge the write. That exposes splits immediately and settles the argument—either the commit log blocks, or the version vectors mismatch.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the dual-log system with a write-through checksum plus a background reconciliation worker now. Two fully independent logs run in parallel, and every record carries a checksum of its content; the worker streams real-time diffs and blocks writes only when mismatches are proven, not suspected. This guarantees no silent corruption and no blind spots, even under races. The trade-off is accepting a small latency hit on writes when reconciliation blocks, but that’s safer than risking user data loss.

name: Scriv
text: The write-through checksum plus background reconciliation still risks silent corruption if the diff worker lags behind a sustained split—user data can diverge for minutes before reconciliation flags it. Instead, run two independent logs with a *write-through version vector* and a *read-time validator*: any read checks both logs for the latest version before returning data; mismatches halt the read and trigger immediate reconciliation. Settle it with a 24-hour chaos test injecting random splits and measuring how long corruption goes undetected.
